Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in interactive settings, such as AI coding assistants, where the input context is not static but undergoes frequent, real-time modifications (insertions and deletions) by the user. Standard autoregressive inference relies heavily on the Key-Value (KV) cache to avoid redundant computation. However, the KV cache mechanism is brittle regarding non-sequential edits: inserting or deleting tokens in the middle of a prompt invalidates the positional information of all subsequent tokens stored in the cache. Consequently, systems are forced into a dilemma: either perform a "full re-computation" of the cache (incurring high latency and computational cost) or naively append new tokens (causing "temporal confusion" where positional indices clash, leading to severe performance degradation). There is currently no efficient method to update the KV cache for non-sequential edits while maintaining correct positional semantics.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that the positional information within the KV cache of modern Transformers—specifically those using Rotary Positional Encoding (RoPE)—can be mathematically decoupled from the semantic content and essentially "moved" without requiring a full forward pass of the model. We propose that by applying a specific linear transformation to the existing cached keys, we can "shift" their encoded positions to reflect the user's edits. This would allow us to reuse the vast majority of the pre-computed cache, correcting only the positional alignment, thereby achieving the accuracy of full re-computation with negligible computational overhead.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose to develop a technique called **Positional Integrity Encoding (PIE)**. This method will operate directly on the cached Key vectors during the inference phase, bypassing the need to re-encode the original token sequence. The workflow is as follows:

1.  **Cache Segmentation:** Upon a user edit (insertion or deletion), we will separate the KV cache into the "pre-edit" segment (which remains valid) and the "post-edit" segment (where positional information is now incorrect).
2.  **Inverse Rotation (Decoupling):** For the post-edit segment, we will design an operation that utilizes the properties of Rotary Positional Embeddings. Conceptually, we will apply an "inverse rotation" matrix to the stored Key vectors. This step aims to strip the incorrect positional bias from the embeddings, reverting them to a position-neutral state.
3.  **Re-Rotation (Realignment):** Immediately following the decoupling, we will apply a new rotation matrix that corresponds to the tokens' *new* indices (shifted forward for insertions or backward for deletions). This effectively "teleports" the semantic information to the correct location in the sequence.
4.  **Integration:** The corrected post-edit cache will be concatenated with the newly computed cache for the inserted text. This results in a unified, positionally consistent KV cache that the attention mechanism can utilize as if it had been generated via a full sequential pass.

This entire process relies solely on lightweight matrix multiplications, avoiding the expensive layer-by-layer transformer computations required by standard re-encoding.

## Expected Contribution
The primary contribution of this research will be a theoretical and practical framework for **malleable KV caches**.
1.  **Theoretical Value:** We expect to demonstrate that positional encoding in Transformers is not an immutable property of the generated embeddings but a reversible attribute that can be manipulated post-hoc.
2.  **Practical Value:** This approach will unlock true real-time interactivity for long-context LLM applications (like IDE copilots). By eliminating the need for full re-computation, we anticipate reducing the latency of cache updates by an order of magnitude, making the system responsive enough for keystroke-level assistance without sacrificing model accuracy.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a comprehensive evaluation framework to assess the efficiency and accuracy of Positional Integrity Encoding (PIE) in real-time code editing scenarios.

*   **Models Utilized:**
    *   **DeepSeek-Coder:** Sizes 1.3B, 6.7B, and 33B.
    *   **CodeLlama:** Sizes 7B and 34B.
*   **Datasets:**
    *   **RepoBench-C-8k:** Utilized the test set for Python and Java languages.
    *   **HumanEval & HumanEval-X:** Used for code generation tasks (Python and C++).
*   **Task Configurations (RepoBench):**
    *   **Cross-File-First (XF-F):** Masking the first appearance of a cross-file line within a file.
    *   **Cross-File-Random (XF-R):** Masking a random, non-first occurrence of a cross-file line.
    *   **In-File (IF):** Masking an in-file line unrelated to cross-file modules.
*   **Simulated Editing Scenarios:**
    *   **Code Insertion:** Randomly deleting 5 consecutive lines to treat them as "inserted" tokens (approx. 64 tokens for Python, 51 for Java).
    *   **Code Deletion:** Inserting 5 random lines to treat them as "deleted" tokens.
    *   **Multi-place Code Edition:** Simultaneous insertion and deletion operations.
*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Accuracy:** Exact Match (EM) and Edit Similarity (ES).
    *   **Efficiency:** Latency (Time in milliseconds) required to encode the edited context.
    *   **Analysis:** Cosine Similarity of key representations and KL Divergence of token distributions.
    *   **Generation:** Pass@1 (for HumanEval).
*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Full-recomputation:** Re-computing the KV cache for all edited and subsequent tokens (Upper bound for accuracy, lower bound for efficiency).
    *   **Conflict Fast Encoding:** Re-computing only edited tokens without adjusting subsequent position indices (Lower bound for accuracy, upper bound for efficiency).
    *   **Reuse Baseline:** Reusing pre-edit context without modification (used in Appendix experiments).
*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Hardware:** Single NVIDIA A100 GPU for 1.3B/6.7B/7B models. Two A100s for encoding and eight A100s for generation for 33B/34B models.
    *   **Decoding:** Greedy decoding strategy generating 64 tokens.
    *   **Batch Size:** 1.
    *   **Repetitions:** All experiments repeated three times with different seeds; averaged scores recorded.
    *   **Codebase:** Hugging Face Transformers.

*   PIE maintained prediction accuracy nearly identical to that of Full-recomputation across various scenarios.
*   In the Cross-File-First (XF-F) setting, the maximum relative difference between PIE and Full-recomputation in terms of Exact Match (EM) was 0.3% for insertion, 0.66% for deletion, and 1.33% for edition.
*   Observation from generation distribution analysis (KL Divergence): The KL divergence between PIE and Full-recomputation predictions was consistently low (below 0.0002) across 64 generated tokens. In contrast, Conflict Fast Encoding showed significantly higher KL divergence (2x larger).

*   Observation from Cosine Similarity analysis: The cosine similarity between key representations of PIE and Full-recomputation was consistently around 1.0 across all model layers.
*   Conversely, the cosine similarity for Conflict Fast Encoding dropped significantly in earlier layers, indicating temporal confusion.

**Ablation and Comparison with Naive Approaches:**
*   Conflict Fast Encoding, while inducing minimal cost, resulted in severe performance drops (e.g., in Python 6.7B XF-F Insertion, EM dropped from ~28.95 to 5.35).
*   PIE effectively mitigated temporal confusion, proving that the semantic impact of minor edits is relatively negligible compared to the structural impact of positional indices.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Large Language Models (LLMs) rely heavily on the Key-Value (KV) cache mechanism to accelerate autoregressive generation. In a static generation setting, this is highly efficient. However, we identify a critical inefficiency in the **real-time editing setting**, a scenario ubiquitous in interactive coding assistants where users frequently insert, delete, or modify code within an existing context.

Currently, when a user edits a sequence (modifying tokens from position $i$ to $j$), the standard approach is **full recomputation**: the model must discard the cache and re-encode the entire sequence from the edit point onwards. This results in significant computational overhead and latency, scaling poorly with sequence length.

The alternative—naively encoding only the edited subsequence and stitching it into the existing cache—fails due to **structural temporal confusion**. Because modern LLMs utilize relative positional encodings (specifically Rotary Positional Encoding, or RoPE), inserting or deleting tokens shifts the relative positions of all subsequent tokens. If the cached keys for the subsequent text are not updated, they retain their old positional indices, causing the model to attend to incorrect relative distances. This leads to a catastrophic drop in prediction accuracy. We define the problem as the need to update the positional information of cached keys efficiently without performing a full forward pass on the unedited suffix of the sequence.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can exploit the algebraic properties of Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) to mathematically "shift" the positional information stored in the KV cache.

We propose **Positional Integrity Encoding (PIE)**. Our core hypothesis is that since RoPE encodes position via rotation matrices, we can correct the positional alignment of the post-edit KV cache by applying a specific inverse rotation (to strip old positional data) followed by a forward rotation (to inject new positional data). This operation can be reduced to a single matrix multiplication applied to the existing cache, theoretically allowing for correct attention calculation with negligible computational cost compared to full recomputation.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will implement a framework that intercepts the KV cache update process during inference. The methodology consists of defining the editing operations and constructing the correction mechanism based on RoPE properties.

### 1. Formulation of the Real-Time Editing Scenario
Let $s = (w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n)$ be the original token sequence. An edit operation replaces the subsequence $w_{[i:j]}$ with a new subsequence of length $m$, denoted as $[a_1, \ldots, a_m]$. The new sequence $s^{edit}$ has a modified length.

We partition the KV cache into three segments:
1.  **Prefix ($1$ to $i$):** Unchanged. We retain $K_{[1:i]}$ and $V_{[1:i]}$.
2.  **Edited Segment ($i+1$ to $i+m$):** New input. We must compute $K_{[i+1:i+m]}^{edit}$ and $V_{[i+1:i+m]}^{edit}$ by feeding the new tokens $[a_1, \ldots, a_m]$ through the model.
3.  **Suffix ($j+1$ to $n$):** Semantically unchanged, but positionally invalid. We possess $K_{[j+1:n]}$ and $V_{[j+1:n]}$ but their internal rotary embeddings correspond to their old indices, not their new indices starting at $i+m+1$.

### 2. Mathematical Derivation of PIE
We build upon the RoPE definition. Given a token vector $x_q$ and $x_k$ at positions $u$ and $v$, the attention score is:
$$ z_{uv} = \pmb{x}_u^T W_q^T \pmb{R}_{v-u} W_k \pmb{x}_v $$
where $\pmb{R}_{v-u}$ is the rotary matrix dependent on relative distance. Crucially, the rotation matrix decomposes as $\pmb{R}_{v-u} = \pmb{R}_u^T \pmb{R}_v$. In the cache, a key vector $k$ at position $idx$ is stored as $\pmb{R}_{idx} W_k x_{idx}$.

To correct the suffix cache $K_{[j+1:n]}$, we must update a key vector $k_{j'}^l$ (where $j'$ is the original index $j' \in [j+1, n]$ and $l$ is the layer) to reflect its new position. The new position index is $i + m + (j' - j)$.

We formulate the correction as a transformation:
$$ \pmb{k}_{j'}^{edit, l} = \pmb{R}_{i+m+j'-j} \pmb{R}_{j'}^{-1} \pmb{k}_{j'}^l $$
Here:
*   $\pmb{R}_{j'}^{-1}$ (or $\pmb{R}_{-j'}$) removes the rotation associated with the *old* position $j'$.
*   $\pmb{R}_{i+m+j'-j}$ applies the rotation for the *new* calculated position.

### 3. Algorithm Simplification and Construction
We will simplify the transformation to minimize operations. By combining the rotation matrices, the update equation becomes:
$$ k_{j'}^{edit, l} = R_{i+m+j'-j} R_{-j'} k_{j'}^l = R_{i+m-j} k_{j'}^l $$
This simplification reveals that we only need to rotate the cached keys by a constant angle determined by the shift magnitude ($i+m-j$).

The construction of the final edited KV cache $\mathcal{K}^{edit}$ and $\mathcal{V}^{edit}$ will proceed as follows:
1.  **Prefix:** Copy $\mathcal{K}_{[1:i]}$.
2.  **Edit:** Compute $\mathcal{K}_{[i+1:i+m]}^{edit}$ via standard forward pass on new tokens.
3.  **Suffix:** Compute $\mathcal{K}_{[j+1:n]}^{edit}$ by applying the transformation matrix $R_{i+m-j}$ to every vector in the existing $\mathcal{K}_{[j+1:n]}$. The Values $\mathcal{V}_{[j+1:n]}$ require no update as they do not contain positional embeddings.

The final cache assembly is:
$$ \mathcal{K}^{edit} = \mathrm{Concat}(\mathcal{K}_{[1:i]}, \mathcal{K}_{[i+1:i+m]}^{edit}, \mathcal{K}_{[j+1:n]}^{edit}) $$
$$ \mathcal{V}^{edit} = \mathrm{Concat}(\mathcal{V}_{[1:i]}, \mathcal{V}_{[i+1:i+m]}^{edit}, \mathcal{V}_{[j+1:n]}) $$

This process requires only a single round of matrix multiplication for the suffix, independent of the model depth's full computation graph.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Theoretical Advancement:** We aim to demonstrate that the positional information in RoPE-based Transformers is decoupled from semantic content and is fully reversible. This establishes a theoretical basis for direct manipulation of the KV cache in vector space.
2.  **Algorithmic Efficiency:** By reducing the complexity of handling edits from $O(N)$ (re-encoding the full suffix) to a constant-time matrix multiplication applied to the cache, we expect to eliminate the latency bottleneck in real-time coding assistants.
3.  **Preservation of Accuracy:** Unlike approximate methods or naive stitching, PIE is mathematically exact regarding positional embeddings. We expect the model's perplexity and next-token prediction capability to remain identical (or near-identical) to the full-recomputation baseline, maintaining "positional integrity" without the computational cost.

notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
